title: After birth: recovery, support and warning signs
intro: The period after birth involves physical healing, learning to care for a newborn and adjusting to interrupted sleep. Recovery varies with the birth, complications and support available. The parent and baby both need follow-up, even when the birth seemed straightforward. This guide focuses on planning care and recognising problems rather than setting a deadline for getting back to normal.

sections.heading: Leave with a plan for both parent and baby
paragraphs: Before going home, ask who will check your recovery, feeding and the baby's health, and whom to contact outside routine hours. Confirm follow-up for blood pressure, anaemia, diabetes or other pregnancy complications where relevant. Arrange transport and practical help with meals, laundry and other children. Screening and home-visit arrangements vary by country; the German services described in the original reference are not automatic entitlements elsewhere. Ask your local team what is available and what appointments need booking.

sections.heading: Support healing without pushing through worsening pain
paragraphs: Vaginal bleeding normally changes and lessens as recovery progresses. Perineal tears, stitches or a caesarean wound may need specific care. Follow your discharge instructions on hygiene, pain relief and activity; check medicine suitability if breastfeeding. Ask for advice about difficulty passing urine, persistent constipation, leakage or painful pelvic-floor exercises. Gentle movement and rest can be balanced according to your condition. Increasing pain, a wound opening or unpleasant-smelling discharge should not be dismissed as something every new parent must endure.

sections.heading: Act promptly on physical warning signs
paragraphs: Heavy or rapidly increasing bleeding, fainting, chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe persistent headache or vision changes need immediate medical attention. A painful swollen leg, fever or severe abdominal pain also needs urgent assessment. Serious complications can begin after discharge, including in someone whose pregnancy blood pressure was normal. Tell the team that you recently gave birth and when. If you are collapsing, severely breathless or otherwise critically unwell, seek emergency help rather than waiting for the next postnatal appointment.

sections.heading: Get feeding help and protect emotional wellbeing
paragraphs: Ask for hands-on feeding support without blame, whether breastfeeding, formula feeding or combining approaches. Persistent breast pain, a hot painful breast with fever or concern that the baby is feeding poorly needs advice. Bonding can develop gradually. Tearfulness may be short-lived, but worsening low mood, anxiety, inability to cope or symptoms that persist deserve professional support. Severe confusion, hallucinations or immediate risk of harm is an emergency. A trusted adult should stay and help keep parent and baby safe while urgent care is arranged.

sections.heading: Use follow-up to discuss more than the wound
paragraphs: Postnatal visits are an opportunity to discuss sleep, mood, birth experiences, continence, sex, contraception and ongoing health conditions. Fertility can return before the first period, and breastfeeding is not automatically reliable contraception. Ask about a method that suits your circumstances. Partners and relatives can support recovery by doing specific tasks and noticing changes, while respecting privacy and choices. If pain, exhaustion or distress stops you managing daily life, ask for an earlier review rather than waiting for a scheduled check.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: practical feeding support
examples.text: A parent has painful feeds and worries about milk intake. They ask the midwife to observe a feed and check the baby rather than simply enduring pain. A relative prepares meals and handles household tasks so the parent can rest and attend follow-up.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: headache after discharge
examples.text: After an apparently uncomplicated birth, a parent develops a severe persistent headache and blurred vision at home. They seek immediate assessment and explicitly mention the recent birth instead of assuming the symptoms are only from lost sleep.

questions: Who is responsible for my follow-up and the baby's checks, and whom do we contact urgently?
Which bleeding, pain, wound or mood changes require assessment before the next appointment?
What support is available for feeding, pelvic-floor symptoms, mental health and contraception?
